interactions.label: Leukoplakia carries a higher risk of malignant transformation than erythroplakia

params.question: Leukoplakia carries a higher risk of malignant transformation than erythroplakia.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect — the statement is false. It is erythroplakia (the red, velvety patch), not leukoplakia, that carries the higher risk of malignant transformation. Early biopsy of erythroplakia always beats watchful waiting.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Erythroplakia, the red velvety patch, carries substantially higher malignant potential than leukoplakia, the white patch. Any erythroplakia found on examination warrants prompt biopsy rather than watchful waiting.

interactions.label: Which statement about HPV-16-associated oropharyngeal cancer, as described in th

params.question: Which statement about HPV-16-associated oropharyngeal cancer, as described in the video, is correct?

answers.text: It typically arises at the base of tongue or tonsil, affects younger non-smoking patients, and carries a better prognosis than tobacco-related disease.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. HPV-16-driven oropharyngeal cancer is a distinct subset arising at the base of tongue and tonsil, typically in younger, non-smoking patients, and it carries a notably better prognosis than tobacco-related squamous cell carcinoma.

answers.text: It is more common in elderly heavy smokers and carries a worse prognosis than tobacco-related disease.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. This describes the classic tobacco-related pattern. HPV-16-driven cancer instead affects younger, non-smoking patients and has a better, not worse, prognosis.

answers.text: It predominantly affects the buccal mucosa rather than the oropharynx.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. Buccal mucosa cancer is the classic site for smokeless tobacco and areca nut chewing. HPV-16 disease arises at the base of tongue and tonsil, within the oropharynx.

answers.text: It shows no association with patient age or smoking status.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. HPV-16-associated disease has a characteristic demographic — younger, non-smoking patients — which distinguishes it clinically from tobacco-driven cancer.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the contrast: tobacco-related cancer skews older/smokers with a worse prognosis, while HPV-16-driven oropharyngeal cancer skews younger/non-smokers with a better prognosis.
Well done — you have correctly identified the HPV-16 oropharyngeal cancer profile: base of tongue/tonsil, younger non-smokers, better prognosis.

interactions.label: Per the '80-80-80 rule' for salivary gland tumours described in the video, which

params.question: Per the '80-80-80 rule' for salivary gland tumours described in the video, which statement is correct?

answers.text: About 80% of salivary tumours arise in the parotid; of those, about 80% are benign; and 80% of the benign ones are pleomorphic adenomas.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is the classic epidemiological rule of thumb: parotid predominance, mostly benign, and pleomorphic adenoma as the commonest benign tumour.

answers.text: About 80% of all salivary tumours are malignant.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. The rule states the opposite — most parotid tumours (about 80%) are benign. Malignancy becomes proportionally more likely in the smaller salivary glands, not the parotid.

answers.text: About 80% of salivary tumours arise in the submandibular gland.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. The parotid, not the submandibular gland, accounts for roughly 80% of salivary tumours. The submandibular gland is instead the site of about 80% of salivary duct stones.

answers.text: About 80% of parotid tumours require total parotidectomy with facial nerve sacrifice.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. Since most parotid tumours are benign, most are treated with nerve-preserving superficial parotidectomy; nerve sacrifice is reserved for tumours directly invading the nerve.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the 80-80-80 rule: about 80% of salivary tumours are parotid, 80% of those are benign, and 80% of those benign tumours are pleomorphic adenomas.
Correct — the 80-80-80 rule: parotid predominance, mostly benign, mostly pleomorphic adenoma.

interactions.label: A patient with oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma is found to have a hard, palp

params.question: A patient with oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma is found to have a hard, palpable cervical lymph node in addition to the primary tumour. Based on the stage-directed treatment framework described, which management approach is most appropriate?

answers.text: Combined modality treatment — surgery with therapeutic neck dissection, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiation.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A palpable, hard neck node signals nodal metastasis and advanced-stage disease, which requires combined modality treatment: surgery including therapeutic neck dissection, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiation.

answers.text: Wide local excision of the primary tumour alone, since the neck node can be observed.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. Wide local excision alone is reserved for early-stage disease without nodal spread. A palpable node must be addressed with neck dissection, not observation.

answers.text: No neck dissection is needed once a node is already palpable, since elective dissection is only for clinically negative necks.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. A clinically involved (palpable, hard) node requires therapeutic neck dissection. Elective dissection is the separate strategy used only when nodes appear clinically clear but occult spread risk is high.

answers.text: Definitive chemoradiation alone, as used for HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. Definitive chemoradiation as the primary approach is described specifically for HPV-driven oropharyngeal cancer. Oral cavity cancer with nodal spread is managed surgically with adjuvant chemoradiation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: nodal involvement upstages disease to advanced stage, shifting management from single-modality surgery to combined surgery, neck dissection, and adjuvant chemoradiation.
Correct — a palpable hard node means advanced-stage disease, treated with surgery plus therapeutic neck dissection and adjuvant chemoradiation.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old woman has a slow-growing, painless swelling in the superficial lob

params.question: A 45-year-old woman has a slow-growing, painless swelling in the superficial lobe of the parotid gland with normal facial nerve function; FNAC confirms pleomorphic adenoma. What is the most appropriate surgical treatment?

answers.text: Superficial parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A benign superficial-lobe parotid tumour such as pleomorphic adenoma is treated with superficial parotidectomy, carefully preserving the facial nerve.
Not correct. Pleomorphic adenoma has microscopic pseudopodia extending beyond its false capsule. Enucleation leaves tumour tissue behind and guarantees recurrence, so it must never be used.

answers.text: Total parotidectomy with sacrifice of the facial nerve.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not correct. Nerve sacrifice is reserved for malignant tumours directly invading the facial nerve. This benign, superficial tumour with intact nerve function needs only superficial parotidectomy with nerve preservation.
Not correct. Submandibular gland excision is the treatment for submandibular tumours or gland damaged by recurrent sialolithiasis, not for a parotid gland tumour.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key pearl: pleomorphic adenoma must never be enucleated because of its pseudopodia — superficial parotidectomy with nerve preservation is the correct operation for a benign superficial-lobe tumour.
Correct — superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation is the answer whenever a benign superficial-lobe parotid tumour is confirmed.
